html:
In 1819, months after the death of Kamehameha I, the rulers of the Kingdom of Hawaii broke the kapu, the sacred laws of the old religion, and ordered the temples and images destroyed.

The kapu system set rules on what people could do, touch and eat, and when. Among the strictest: men and women could not eat together, and women could not eat foods such as pork and most bananas. Breaking a kapu could mean death. Trade and contact with foreigners, who broke kapu without harm, had weakened belief in it.

Kamehameha's widow Kaʻahumanu, now co regent, and his widow Keōpūolani, mother of the new king, pushed for change. The young king Kamehameha II, Liholiho, sat down to eat with the women at a public feast, an act called ʻai noa, free eating. The high priest Hewahewa supported it. A cousin who defended the old gods was defeated in battle. The first American missionaries arrived in April 1820 to find the old religion gone, which made their work much easier. Compare Missionaries reach Tahiti.
sum: In 1819, months after the death of Kamehameha I, the rulers of the Kingdom of Hawaii broke the kapu, the sacred laws of the old religion, and ordered the temples and images destroyed.
